title: A dependable neural communication channel for profound paralysis

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a neural interface through which a person with profound paralysis can reliably communicate what they intend to say, even when speech and movement cannot provide a usable channel. The intended capability is open-ended, self-directed conversation: the user chooses when to communicate, produces messages, recognizes errors and corrects them. Dependability includes being able to use the system in everyday life without continuous researcher assistance. These are proposed capabilities, not achievements established by the supplied evidence.

As a design synthesis, the communication channel includes more than a decoder that converts brain activity into words or cursor actions. It also requires usable activation and stopping controls, feedback that lets the person check the output, a practical correction method and sustained operation as circumstances change. The central goal is decoding intended communication; it does not require general access to private thoughts, a theory of consciousness or repair of the underlying neurological disease.

significance.text: Conditionally, dependable communication would restore a fundamental capability to people whose neurological condition prevents them from expressing themselves through speech or movement. Being able to initiate a conversation, ask a question, express a preference or correct a misunderstanding would have direct value even if the interface restored no movement and did not alter disease progression. The revolutionary advance would be making that capability consistently available under the user's control.

As a reasoned downstream possibility, independent everyday use could expand participation in relationships, education, work and decisions about care. These benefits would depend on accessibility, usability, affordability and sustained technical and clinical support. A successful laboratory decoder alone would not establish those outcomes, and successful use by one person would not establish suitability for everyone with profound paralysis.

The appropriate analogy is an assistive communication channel. Decoding a person's deliberate attempt to communicate would not demonstrate unrestricted reading of their thoughts, memories or beliefs. Nor would successful communication establish recovery of the biological pathways responsible for speech or movement. These distinctions limit the interpretation of both the proposed impact and any future demonstration.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is dependable, sustained communication across a clinically meaningful range of users, settings and disease stages. Proposed practical requirements include stable decoding, user-controlled activation, effective error correction and operation without continuous researcher intervention. The supplied scientific text does not establish these as published consensus requirements; they are a coherent engineering formulation of the intended goal.

As an engineering synthesis, concrete barriers include obtaining sufficiently informative neural signals, converting them into intended messages with useful speed and accuracy, and maintaining performance when signals or the user's condition change. A practical system must also distinguish deliberate communication from periods when no output is intended. Adaptation and recalibration would need to remain manageable for a person with very limited movement and could not depend on an inaccessible correction or setup procedure.

Dependable use also requires solving the interaction and maintenance problems surrounding decoding. The user needs an accessible way to inspect output, reject an unintended message, repair an error and stop communication. For an implanted implementation, proposed engineering and clinical concerns include durable recording, hardware maintenance, procedural complications and the burden of long-term support. These are design considerations inferred from the proposed capability, not findings verified in the supplied Card report.

Generalization remains a separate challenge from achieving strong performance in an individual. Differences in the cause and progression of paralysis, available neural signals, fatigue and communication needs may affect training and operation. A convincing advance would establish which users and conditions the system serves, what assistance remains necessary and where performance fails, rather than assuming that one successful configuration transfers to every person.

current_state.text: The supplied research metadata identifies a report attributed to Card and colleagues, dated 15 June 2026, titled “Long-term independent use of an intracortical brain-computer interface for speech and cursor control,” with DOI 10.1038/s41591-026-04414-6 and a supplied PubMed URL. The research account describes independent home use of a speech and cursor interface by one person with ALS. That is the reported achievement in the supplied account, but its participant details, capabilities, duration and publication details cannot be independently verified from the retained source text described by the review.

The review found that the retained source artifact contained only a cookie-access notice, with neither an abstract nor article text. It therefore did not verify the intended document's identity or scientific results. Although the source index records the artifact as saved and verified, those inventory fields do not supply the missing scientific content. The earlier statement that the abstract had been inspected, and that a separate full-text page was blocked, cannot be sustained from the retained evidence.

If the supplied account is confirmed, independent home operation by one participant would represent meaningful progress toward practical communication. It would still leave open performance across other users and causes of paralysis, the extent of remaining assistance, durability and safety at scale. The supplied materials provide no verifiable communication-rate, accuracy, uptime, follow-up-duration or complication figures. The access limitation does not establish that the reported result is false.

The research also compares the report with an earlier six-command demonstration, but no source for that earlier result is supplied. The claimed progression beyond it therefore remains unverified. The review's freshness record is empty, so the materials cannot establish a comprehensive state of the field as of 1 November 2026 or identify later developments. They also do not provide enough scientific text to resolve publication or peer-review status, independent replication, or whether access limitations extended beyond the retained copy.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing evidence would come from multicenter studies in which people with diverse causes of severe paralysis independently conduct open-ended conversations over years, including at home. Participation should be broad enough to test relevant differences in disease, residual movement and progression, while reporting exclusions and unsuccessful cases. Such studies would establish demonstrated breadth within the tested population and conditions, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Diverse participants sustain independent, open-ended home conversations over years

completion_criteria.text: The proposed demonstration should define independence before testing. Reports should distinguish user-operated communication from sessions requiring a researcher to start the system, recalibrate decoding, correct messages or recover from failures. They should account for caregiver help, scheduled technical support, setup time and interruptions. User-controlled activation, stopping and correction should be tested through functions accessible to the intended participants.
completion_criteria.label: User-controlled communication demonstrated with full accounting of assistance required

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reliability measures should include successful communication of intended messages, errors and their consequences, correction success and effort, unintended output, communication speed, availability and recovery after failures. Open-ended conversation should be distinguished from prompted tasks or selection among a small fixed set of commands. Numerical targets should be justified against participants' needs and available alternatives; no such targets are established standards in the supplied materials.
completion_criteria.label: Open-ended communication reliability quantified with justified numerical targets

completion_criteria.text: Longitudinal evaluation should document performance changes, retraining needs, maintenance, adverse events and the burden placed on users and supporters. Acceptable complication rates require explicit definitions and a benefit–risk assessment appropriate to the population and implementation. Reproducibility would require sufficiently described methods and independent evaluation across sites, with practical boundaries reported clearly, including users, environments and disease stages for which dependable communication has not been shown.
completion_criteria.label: Longitudinal dependability independently evaluated across sites with practical limits reported

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: NRL-17, a durable bidirectional neural interface for movement and sensation, has the closest engineering overlap through long-term neural interfacing and dependable user control. NRL-07 centers on expressing intended communication; NRL-17 centers on movement and sensory feedback. NRL-08, a visual-cortex prosthesis, likewise concerns an engineered neural interface, but its defining output is useful sight. Shared interface challenges do not make these capabilities interchangeable.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-02, a predictive theory of neural circuit computation, could inform interpretation of neural signals, while NRL-03, whole-brain cellular-resolution recording, concerns a much broader measurement capability. NRL-07 need not await either a general computational theory or whole-brain recording if a more limited signal supports useful communication. NRL-01, a theory of consciousness, addresses a different explanatory problem; successful communication decoding would not by itself resolve it.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-05, functional spinal-cord reconnection, and NRL-06, replacement of lost brain tissue while preserving learned function, seek biological restoration. NRL-07 could provide communication despite persistent neurological impairment. NRL-16, biological repair of the injured visual pathway, is similarly distinct from an assistive communication channel. NRL-04, reading and selectively repairing specific memory traces, concerns memory content and intervention; intended-message decoding does not establish either capability.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-10, programmable delivery to selected brain cells, concerns biological targeting and is not an inherent prerequisite for this communication concept. The disease-focused goals in NRL-09, NRL-11, NRL-12, NRL-13, NRL-14, NRL-15 and NRL-18 concern prevention, protection or treatment of neurological disease. Their success could change communication needs or eligibility, but a dependable channel would remain a distinct functional achievement and would not demonstrate control of those disease processes.

unresolved_issues: The retained artifact cannot verify the Card report's identity, date, authorship, DOI, publication status or scientific findings.
The reported ALS participant, independent home operation, speech and cursor capabilities, follow-up duration and remaining assistance require usable source text.
Quantitative performance, maintenance burden, adverse events and complication rates are not established by the supplied evidence.
The earlier six-command demonstration lacks a supplied source, preventing verification of the claimed comparison.
The empty freshness record prevents a comprehensive assessment of the field as of 1 November 2026 or of subsequent developments.
Proposed completion criteria still require study-specific definitions and justified targets for independence, reliability, meaningful communication and acceptable risk.

brief.title: Dependable conversation despite profound paralysis
possible: People who cannot speak or move could start a conversation, ask a question or correct a misunderstanding through their brain signals. They would choose what to say, check the words and repair mistakes, without a researcher continuously helping them.
why: Being able to express a preference or make decisions about care would restore a basic part of independence. Dependable everyday communication could also help people take part in relationships, education and work.

sources.showed: An implanted brain–computer interface (BCI), which turns brain signals into computer output, let a man with paralysis converse and use his computer at home. A care partner helped with hardware and startup.
sources.quote: He labeled 92% of sentences as being decoded at least mostly correctly.
sources.cited_for: The study demonstrates sustained home communication without researchers present.
sources.not_established: Success in this participant does not establish dependable communication across different users or causes of paralysis.

sources.showed: The researchers reported independent home use by 14 people with paralysis. They measured spelling accuracy, system availability and the help needed to operate it.
sources.cited_for: The study supports home use across participants and shows why assistance and interruptions need to be measured.
sources.not_established: Spelling tasks and months of home use do not establish years of dependable, open-ended conversation across causes of paralysis.

sources.showed: A participant used an implanted communication system at home for 7 years. Use ended as control became unreliable and brain signals weakened.
sources.quote: At-home use ended when BCI control became unreliable. There were no signs of technical malfunction.
sources.cited_for: The study demonstrates prolonged home use while exposing a limit to durability as disease progresses.
sources.not_established: It does not establish sustained open-ended conversation or prove that disease progression caused the loss of control.

sources.showed: An implanted system converted a participant’s attempted speech into text at 62 words per minute. It could draw on a large vocabulary, although errors remained.
sources.quote: Here we demonstrate a speech-to-text BCI that records spiking activity from intracortical microelectrode arrays.
sources.cited_for: The study demonstrates rapid conversion of attempted speech into words.
sources.not_established: A demonstration in a participant does not establish dependable, independent home conversation over years.

shown: Card and colleagues demonstrated nearly two years of home communication and computer use by a man with paralysis. He conversed with family and friends and maintained full-time employment. Researchers were absent during home use, while a care partner helped with setup.

Vansteensel and colleagues demonstrated longer use of a simpler implanted communication system. It eventually became unreliable as brain signals weakened. Together, these results show both practical progress and the challenge of keeping communication dependable.
missing: Studies have yet to establish years of independent conversation across diverse causes and stages of profound paralysis.
Dependable use still needs accessible starting, stopping and correction controls, with all remaining assistance accounted for.
Long-term safety, maintenance and reliability need independent evaluation across research sites.

milestones.label: Diverse participants sustain independent home conversations over years
milestones.explanation: Studies across centers would have to demonstrate years of independent, open-ended home conversation across diverse causes of paralysis. This would establish whom the system can serve.

milestones.label: Users control communication with all assistance accounted for
milestones.explanation: Testing would have to demonstrate accessible starting, stopping and correction while accounting for setup, caregiver help and technical support. This would establish how independently users can communicate.

milestones.label: Conversation reliability meets justified numerical targets
milestones.explanation: Testing would have to measure intended messages, errors, correction, unintended output, speed, availability and recovery against justified targets. This would establish whether conversation meets users’ needs.

milestones.label: Independent evaluations establish long-term dependability and practical limits
milestones.explanation: Independent studies across sites would have to track performance, retraining, maintenance, harms and support burdens over time. This would establish durability, acceptable risk and the conditions where communication fails.

uncertain: How well will systems transfer between people with different causes of paralysis and changing disease stages?
Which measures and thresholds best capture useful conversation, independence and acceptable risk?
Can communication remain reliable when brain signals weaken over time?

page.title: Implanted brain–computer interfaces for home communication
page.definition: An implanted brain–computer interface (BCI) lets a person with severe paralysis compose and correct messages at home. Implanted electrodes record deliberate changes in brain activity. Software can turn an attempted hand movement into a click that selects a letter, or turn attempted speech into text or a synthetic voice. A caregiver may set up the equipment. Trial participants have used such systems at home without a researcher present.

goal.need: In a US survey of 216 people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), 36 could no longer speak. Eye tracking can support spelling until voluntary gaze control deteriorates. Scalp electrodes offer another route, but fitting and removing the cap takes a helper’s time at each use. With an implant, a person who can still control a detectable brain signal could start a conversation with family, send a message or call a caregiver even after losing reliable eye movement. Progressive disease can also erode control of the brain signal.

completion.title: FDA authorises an implanted BCI for home communication by people with severe paralysis.
completion.criterion: FDA grants marketing authorisation for an implanted BCI whose labelled intended use includes self-directed communication at home by people with severe paralysis without continuous researcher supervision. Authorisation must cover the communication system and this use, including prescribed caregiver assistance, through the applicable premarket pathway. The decision must establish reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness. Authorisation of recording electrodes alone or permission to conduct an investigational study does not meet this test.
completion.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, medical-device marketing pathways and implanted-BCI guidance.
completion.threshold_quote: the device is safe and effective for its intended use or uses.
completion.basis: This endpoint requires both a US marketing decision for the labelled home-communication use and reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness. FDA applies that assurance standard to premarket approval and considers it in De Novo classification. A humanitarian device exemption is exempt from the premarket approval requirement to demonstrate effectiveness. The Layer 7-T clearance covers temporary cortical electrodes for use in a professional healthcare environment. In October 2026 NIH reported that implanted speech BCIs remained available only through clinical trials.

milestones.title: An implanted BCI sustains neural recording in vivo through chronic implantation.
milestones.criterion: For a device intended for chronic implantation, assess recording performance periodically over the implantation period using a quantitative measure such as signal-to-noise ratio or spike amplitude. The study duration and number of animals depend on the device risks and available evidence. Relevant prior in vivo evidence, including studies of the same or a similar electrode configuration, may establish performance.
milestones.set_by: FDA, May 2021 implanted-BCI guidance, section III.N; a nonbinding recommendation.
milestones.threshold_quote: long-term device performance should be established in a biological environment

milestones.title: An early human study demonstrates communication by implanted BCI and collects initial safety data.
milestones.criterion: In an authorised early-feasibility study, demonstrate that a participant can use the implanted system for its proposed communication function and collect initial clinical safety data for that device. The study protocol specifies the functional task and safety observations.
milestones.set_by: FDA, May 2021 implanted-BCI guidance, section II; a nonbinding recommendation.
milestones.threshold_quote: proof of the principle and initial clinical safety data

milestones.title: A user copies a 30-character sentence by neural switch within 30 minutes with at most 20% errors.
milestones.criterion: For Utrecht level 2, the user copies a predefined 30-character sentence with a scanning keyboard within 30 minutes, with at most 20% faulty characters. The system must detect an intended switch signal within 10 seconds during spelling. A caregiver may enable or disable the device. The research team administers the copy test during a scheduled visit.
milestones.set_by: UMC Utrecht, NCT02224469 protocol, version 22.0, 14 May 2024, sections 8.1.1 and 8.3.9. Written for a cortical-surface BCI; this is a protocol-specific benchmark.
milestones.threshold_quote: copying a 30 character sentence within 30 minutes, with a margin of maximally 20% faulty characters

milestones.title: A person with paralysis enables and disables BCI communication through brain signals without help.
milestones.criterion: For Utrecht level 3, the user produces a sequence of neural switch commands to move the speller from standby to active mode and back without external help. This permits the user to initiate communication at any time of day or night. The protocol specifies no numerical accuracy threshold and does not formally test this level.
milestones.set_by: UMC Utrecht, NCT02224469 protocol, version 22.0, 14 May 2024, sections 8.1.1 and 8.3.9. Written for a cortical-surface BCI; this is a protocol-specific capability criterion.
milestones.threshold_quote: capable of enabling/disabling AT device control by himself

milestones.title: A pivotal study demonstrates clinical benefit and characterises safety for home communication.
milestones.criterion: A pivotal study demonstrates clinical benefit for the intended population and characterises safety under realistic home-use conditions. The protocol prespecifies endpoints, success criteria and statistical analyses. Where caregivers assist, assess their safety and ability to perform the required tasks. FDA recommends at least one year of long-term follow-up to assess electrode effectiveness and detect late safety signals.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Design Considerations for Pivotal Clinical Investigations for Medical Devices, section 6, and implanted-BCI guidance, section IV. These are nonbinding recommendations.
milestones.threshold_quote: A long-term follow up period of at least 1 year is recommended

milestones.title: A user answers at least 16 of 20 yes/no questions by neural switch on each of two visits.
milestones.criterion: For Utrecht level 1, administer the supervised Communication Channel Verification Questionnaire. Each of 20 questions has a known answer. Present yes and no in two consecutive 30-second windows in random order. The user activates the neural switch in the intended window and withholds it in the other. Require at least 80% correct on each of two visits with at least one control signal. The protocol discontinues training if the user has not reached this level within 28 weeks of implantation.
milestones.set_by: UMC Utrecht, NCT02224469, version 22.0, sections 8.1.1 and 8.3.9. This is a cortical-surface switch protocol.

milestones.title: A user communicates at home between research visits with at most caregiver setup assistance.
milestones.criterion: Document use of the implanted system for the user’s own communication at home between research visits. A caregiver may set up or activate the equipment. Distinguish communication from training and report the frequency and duration of use. The Utrecht protocol sets no minimum number of sessions or hours for this measure.
milestones.set_by: UMC Utrecht, NCT02224469, version 22.0, home-use objective and sections 8.3.8, 8.3.13 and 10.2 on patterns of use.
milestones.threshold_quote: at home without the aid of researchers or other experts (but with minimal caregiver assistance)

not_found: Searches of FDA guidance, NIH material and registered protocols found no universal numerical threshold for conversational accuracy, communication rate, availability or years of independent home use.
No published pivotal home-communication BCI study reporting successful prespecified safety and effectiveness endpoints was found.
No FDA marketing authorisation covering an implanted home-communication BCI was found in FDA-site searches and current NIH material.
Searches of government technology assessments and professional-society guidance found no statement judging implanted home communication unachievable or unworthy of pursuit.

results.finding: One participant had intracortical neural activity recorded on post-implant day 119.
results.detail: The paper reports recording after implantation but does not report the safety or tissue-assessment evidence needed to establish this criterion.
results.quote: Example spike waveforms detected during a 10-s time window are plotted for each electrode (data were recorded on post-implant day 119).

results.finding: One participant with ALS achieved a 23.8% word error rate using a 125,000-word vocabulary.
results.detail: The pilot-trial result demonstrates human speech-decoding proof of principle. This paper cites separate safety data but does not report its own clinical safety outcomes.
results.quote: T12 achieved a 9.1% word error rate for the 50-word vocabulary across all vocalizing days (11.2% for silent) and a 23.8% word error rate for the 125,000-word vocabulary across all vocalizing days (24.7% for silent).

results.finding: One participant copying prompted sentences achieved a 23.8% word error rate.
results.detail: The evaluation used attempted speech and word errors, not the specified 30-character test or neural switches; the participant pressed a button to finalize output.
results.quote: T12 achieved a 9.1% word error rate for the 50-word vocabulary across all vocalizing days (11.2% for silent) and a 23.8% word error rate for the 125,000-word vocabulary across all vocalizing days (24.7% for silent).

results.finding: Four endovascular BCI recipients completed 12 months of follow-up without serious adverse events.
results.detail: All participants controlled a computer with the BCI; the study had ethics approval. Eight mild adverse device effects resolved without intervention.
results.quote: Each completed 12-month follow-up with no serious adverse events and no vessel occlusion or device migration.

results.finding: Four implanted patients maintained stable neural signal bandwidth over 12 months.
results.detail: The first-in-human study also reported no serious adverse events, vessel occlusion, or device migration during follow-up.
results.quote: The mean (SD; range) signal bandwidth for the 4 patients was 233 (16; 206-245) Hz. Bandwidth remained stable throughout the 12-month period, with SDs across all sessions ranging from 7 to 32 Hz for the 4 patients

results.finding: Four implanted patients completed 12-month follow-up with no serious adverse events.
results.detail: This was a first-in-human safety and feasibility study, not a pivotal clinical investigation; it did not involve formal hypothesis testing.

results.quote: Example spike waveforms detected during a 10-s time window are plotted for each electrode (data were recorded on post-implant day 119).

results.finding: One participant with advanced ALS used the implanted BCI for home communication, with availability reaching 20–24 hours per day.
results.detail: Logged hours measure connected availability. The logs omit message contents, use by application, and accuracy. After a BCI-initiated caregiver call, the participant typically used residual mouth movement to answer follow-up questions.
results.quote: In the subsequent 11 months, the participant used the BCI system 20–24 hours per day, mainly to call the caregiver.

results.finding: Across 55 intracortical Utah arrays in 17 macaques and 2 humans, available recordings lasted an average of 622 days.
results.detail: The retrospective study sampled at uneven intervals. Some recordings ended when experiments concluded, so available recording duration can underestimate functional implant life.
results.quote: the average lifespan of available recordings from UEAs was 622 days

results.finding: Connexus-representative implants in two sheep maintained stable spike signal-to-noise ratio over four years.
results.detail: The six-sheep full-platform study provides additional chronic recording evidence. The release summarizes stability across follow-up without reporting visit-level values.
results.quote: Across the four-year study period, spike signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) remained stable in both animals, meaning neural spikes remained clearly distinguishable from background noise years after implantation.

results.finding: In two sheep with epidural WIMAGINE implants, effective ECoG bandwidth remained near 230 Hz during usable follow-up.
results.detail: The impact reduced contact between the electrode array and the dura, increased noise and caused a sharp drop in effective bandwidth before explantation.
results.quote: Based on weekly recordings of raw ECoG signals, the effective bandwidth was in the range of 230 Hz for both animals and remarkably stable over time, meaning preservation of the high frequency bands valuable for decoding of the brain activity using BCIs.

results.finding: In a 10-sheep cohort, endovascular stentrodes sustained stable resting EEG recording bandwidth for up to 190 days.
results.detail: The prototype used a percutaneous lead. Wire fractures limited recordings to 28 days in a separate evoked-potential cohort.
results.quote: demonstrate neural recordings in freely moving sheep for up to 190 d.

results.finding: In five participants with ALS, the endovascular Stentrode sustained neural recording for up to 12 months.
results.detail: The participant with resting-state and impedance data only had 6 months of follow-up.
results.quote:
The data presented herein demonstrates stable neural signals recorded with an endovascular BCI in 
three participants over a year and two participants over six months of follow up.

results.finding: One participant with ALS averaged 91% target-task accuracy across repeated tests of a chronic subdural BCI.
results.detail: Task accuracy reflects recording, decoding, and user performance together.
results.quote:
The patient’s performance on the target task was correct a mean (±SD) of 91±6% of the time 
(83 runs were performed between day 15 and day 262).

results.finding: One participant with locked-in ALS typed about two letters per minute using the implanted BCI.
results.detail: The study used dictated-word spelling to assess communication and documented the immediate postoperative course.
results.quote:
the 
patient accurately and independently controlled a computer typing program 28 weeks after 
electrode placement, at the equivalent of two letters per minute.

results.finding: One participant with ALS averaged 89% response accuracy in supervised neural-switch spelling.
results.detail: Correctly withholding a click counted toward accuracy, so the response accuracy cannot establish the proportion of faulty characters.
results.quote:
From day 168 to day 262, a total of 44 spelling runs were performed during research visits, 
and the patient’s performance was correct 89±6% of the time (Fig. 3, and Fig. S4 in the 
Supplementary Appendix).

results.finding: One participant with locked-in ALS used the implanted BCI for self-directed communication on 32 days.
results.quote:
Logs from the patient’s system indicated that from day 197 (when she received the home-
use system) through day 266, she used the system for communication on 32 days (Fig. 3B) 
and for 86 minutes per day on average.

results.finding: In one cortical-surface ECoG participant, a fixed decoder averaged 96.8% accuracy across follow-up sessions.

results.quote: Across 19 sessions after freezing the classifier, we observed a mean classification accuracy of 96.8% (99% CI [94.5, 98.6]), with accuracies of 100% obtained on eight of these sessions.

results.finding: One participant with quadriplegia and anarthria used a cortical-surface BCI for real-time text decoding at a median 78.3 words per minute.
results.detail: The surgical observation covers initial perioperative safety. The authors state that the data presented do not support conclusions about the trial's primary safety endpoints.

results.finding: One participant demonstrated real-time decoding of self-chosen sentences at home.

results.finding: One participant with ALS retained viable cortical-surface ECoG recording after more than 2 years.
results.detail: The paper refers to Supplementary Note 1 for recording viability. The supplied text does not include that note.

results.finding: One CortiCom participant with ALS used the implanted BCI for spelling and had zero device- or study-related adverse events.
results.detail: The phase I protocol used exploratory outcomes and did not prespecify detailed assessment methods or statistical analyses.
results.quote: To date, there have been no adverse events related to the study device or study participation, and the participant has consented to continue the study.

results.finding: One participant with ALS copied prompted sentences by neural switch at a median of 10.2 correct characters per minute.
results.detail: The task used language-model autocomplete and required the participant to delete mistakes. The paper reports aggregate rates rather than the elapsed time and faulty-character count for a specified 30-character sentence.
results.quote: Using a click detector to navigate a switch scanning speller interface, the study participant can maintain a median spelling rate of 10.2 characters per min.

results.finding: Intracortical arrays recorded neural activity in four participants, with recordings extending to post-implant day 995.
results.detail: Threshold-crossing rates and spike-band power were used as decoding features. The paper does not report longitudinal signal-to-noise ratio, spike amplitude, or an equivalent recording-quality measure.
results.quote: Data are reported from post-implant days 412–995.

results.finding: Three participants with severe dysarthria used an implanted BCI to decode cued inner speech in real time, with a best word error rate of 14%.
results.detail: The 14% result came from the limited-vocabulary evaluation. The paper describes the functional task and trial approvals but gives no device-related adverse-event data.
results.quote: For an initial feasibility test using a limited 50-word vocabulary, we achieved word error rates (WERs) of 24% (95% CI: [18.5%, 28.0%]), 14% ([9.9%, 20.2%]), and 33% ([21.8%, 41.1%]) for T12, T15, and T16, respectively

results.finding: One participant with ALS used an imagined keyword to gate BCI output with 98.75% accuracy.
results.detail: The decoder suppressed output on trials without the keyword. Withholding the keyword while output was already locked did not test a user-commanded transition back to standby.
results.quote: In real-time tests with T12, the keyword was correctly detected (or correctly not detected) with 98.75% accuracy (95% CI: 93.23%-99.97%).

1
; Fig.
1
).

results.finding: One participant with late-stage ALS made intentional BCI caregiver calls on 58% of logged nights.
results.detail: Caregivers logged intentional and unintended activations and missed calls. These logs characterise device operation.
results.quote: 58% of nights contained true positive nocturnal caregiver calls and on average there were 2.3 caregiver calls in those nights.

results.finding: One participant with late-stage ALS used the implanted BCI at home on 494 nights.
results.detail: The 494 nights count all home use. Actual requests were documented in caregiver logs, which ended in April 2022 as caregivers became unable to verify call intent reliably.
results.quote: Between September 2020 and October 2022, the participant used the BCI in 494 nights.

results.finding: One participant with late-stage ALS activated the BCI caregiver-call function in 13 of 14 supervised repetitions.
results.detail: The nightmode sequence enabled a caregiver call. The reported activation task did not test returning the active speller to standby through neural commands.

results.finding: In 1 man with ALS, intracortical recordings supported BCI use over almost 2 years.

results.quote: Nicholas Card and colleagues describe the near-daily home use of a multimodal BCI over almost 2 years by a man with severe paralysis and speech difficulties caused by ALS.

results.finding: One man with ALS communicated 183,060 sentences using an implanted intracortical BCI.

copy sentences displayed on the screen (15 evaluation sessions in total).

results.quote:

sessions run from 8/27/2004 - 10/12/2004.

study-related complications have

results.finding: One participant with severe paralysis used a cortical-surface BCI for streaming synthesized speech with a median onset latency of 1.67 seconds.

results.quote: For the 1024-word-General set, we achieved median latencies of 1.67 s (99% CI [1.57, 1.81]) for speech synthesis and 1.56 s (99% CI [1.4, 1.56]) for text decoding, respectively.

results.finding: Consistent BCI decoding throughout follow-up was reported in 4 of 6 COMMAND participants.

results.quote:
Four out of six 
participants demonstrated consistent BCI decoding p erformance, enabling them to successfully perform 
various digital device control tasks throughout the  one-year post-implant evaluation period.

results.quote:

results.finding: In one participant with ALS, more than 90% of electrodes on each intracortical array continued to detect spiking during chronic implantation.

results.finding: One BrainGate2 participant with ALS achieved 99.2% word accuracy in prompted copying with an intracortical speech BCI.

results.finding: One participant with ALS logged more than 3,800 hours of home BCI use, including self-directed communication.
results.detail: The total includes computer use and idle time. The participant used the BCI for conversations, video calls, email and text messages.
results.quote: Over a 19-month period, the participant used the system in his home for more than 3,800 h, speaking more than 183,000 sentences, browsing the internet, managing personal and professional communications and maintaining full-time employment.

results.finding: Intracortical arrays in one participant with ALS supplied usable speech signals for more than eight months.

word error rate of 2.5% (95% CI, 1.0% to 4.5%) by session 15, and this
approximate accuracy was maintained through session 84, more than eight months

events, and the participant was discharged on postoperative day 3.

results.finding: One participant with ALS averaged 2.5% word error when copying prompted sentences with an implanted speech decoder.

In this

results.finding: One participant with ALS used an intracortical speech BCI at home on 29 session days devoted solely to personal use.
results.detail: A researcher had to connect and launch the system. Three personal-use days included requested recalibration. The reported 248.3 hours combine structured research and personal use.

Across the 29 session days, during which the
participant used the neuroprosthesis solely for personal use, he requested to
recalibrate and update the decoder on three occasions because there were more
errors than he was accustomed to.

results.finding: An endovascular stentrode recorded cortical activity in freely moving sheep for up to 190 days (chronic recording cohort size unspecified).

results.quote: We achieved implantation into a superficial cortical vein overlying the motor cortex via catheter angiography and demonstrate neural recordings in freely moving sheep for up to 190 d.

results.finding: Four Stentrode recipients completed 12 months of safety follow-up in a study that reported home use and perceived communication benefits.

rest data was recorded over periods of 329, 90, and 90 weeks and BCI control data over periods of

definition = "An implanted brain\u2013computer interface (BCI) lets a person with severe paralysis compose and correct messages at home. Implanted electrodes record deliberate changes in brain activity. Software can turn an attempted hand movement into a click that selects a letter, or turn attempted speech into text or a synthetic voice. A caregiver may set up the equipment. Trial participants have used such systems at home without a researcher present.". Reason: The definition gains concrete examples of how a user selects letters or produces speech and distinguishes a working home prototype from the regulatory endpoint.

goal.need = "In a US survey of 216 people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), 36 could no longer speak. Eye tracking can support spelling until voluntary gaze control deteriorates. Scalp electrodes offer another route, but fitting and removing the cap takes a helper\u2019s time at each use. With an implant, a person who can still control a detectable brain signal could start a conversation with family, send a message or call a caregiver even after losing reliable eye movement. Progressive disease can also erode control of the brain signal.". Reason: The existing paragraph reports a spelling study but omits the scale of speech loss, the limits of gaze control and what independent communication makes possible.

add statement by National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders, 2018: "faster and more versatile BCI control techniques for home use". Reason: The 2018 award identifies a public funder, a specific implant programme and an explicit home-use objective.

edit completion: basis = "This endpoint requires both a US marketing decision for the labelled home-communication use and reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness. FDA applies that assurance standard to premarket approval and considers it in De Novo classification. A humanitarian device exemption is exempt from the premarket approval requirement to demonstrate effectiveness. The Layer 7-T clearance covers temporary cortical electrodes for use in a professional healthcare environment. In October 2026 NIH reported that implanted speech BCIs remained available only through clinical trials."; refs = [4, 5, 6, 35, 2]. Reason: The basis currently treats all marketing authorisations as equivalent evidence of effectiveness and omits the actual scope of a cortical-electrode clearance.

edit m1: criterion = "For a device intended for chronic implantation, assess recording performance periodically over the implantation period using a quantitative measure such as signal-to-noise ratio or spike amplitude. The study duration and number of animals depend on the device risks and available evidence. Relevant prior in vivo evidence, including studies of the same or a similar electrode configuration, may establish performance."; threshold_quote = "long-term device performance should be established in a biological environment"; threshold_ref = 6; refs = [6]. Reason: The sheep study’s duration appears inside the test, while FDA specifies periodic quantitative recording over implantation and allows relevant prior evidence.

edit m2: title = "An early human study demonstrates communication by implanted BCI and collects initial safety data."; criterion = "In an authorised early-feasibility study, demonstrate that a participant can use the implanted system for its proposed communication function and collect initial clinical safety data for that device.
